I had read the book, and I thought it would be a good movie the first time I saw it. I'm afraid to say that I was disappointed. The movie did not follow the book and made some changes that I did not like. One of the changes that I did not like the way that Lord Fenton was portrayed. It made no sense to make him out to be a bad man. I felt that the relationship between Lord Fenton and Marianne was not a romantic, and their physical relationship was not intimate. There was also a lot of confrontation between Julia and Lord Fenton in the movie that was not present in the book. The movie portrayed the two in two completely different ways and they did not seem to cross paths often enough to make it seem like there still could be love. I enjoyed the movie, but I believe that it certainly could have been better than it was, had it more true to Alexandra Smith's book..

Set in 1945, Skenbart follows a drunken Swedish bookkeeper who decides to take a train from Stockholm to Berlin. Unfortunately for those around him, he's a walking time bomb, causing trouble everywhere he goes. The train also holds a man and his six-year-old daughter, the man's wife (who's also on the train), a soldier on his way home, two gay old gentlemen, an angry train conductor, two nuns, a group of students, and even a priest. Meant as a mix of post-of-war drama (which it tries to is - at least to begin with) and comedy, the film fails at both. It doesn't feel right as the tone changes from serious drama to comedy, and as the train races towards its final destination, the story becomes more and more bizarre, with the film losing any the drama and a few good bits of comedy in a myriad of pointless plots and characters. The cast itself is packed with famous Swedish actors, no matter how small their roles are. It's like the director called everyone they've ever worked with and offered them a part in the film. Of course, their performances are just as bad as the script (actress lines are terrible, to example). The comedy is more situational than slapstick, with the same jokes repeated over and over. The pacing is incredibly slow at times (quite often, actually), with on scene in particular dragging on for over ten minutes for no good reason. The screenwriter also seems to think that swearing is a good way to replace good dialogue. The film has some nice visuals in moody B&W, but it's wasted on such inept film-making in every other aspect. [2/5]

This movie fails at at everything, even at being bad. Still, it has a strange, cheesy sort of charm.

John Hurt is again Crisp (come on who else could play the part?) and what a performance he gives. Some may say otherwise, but for me Hurt is both brilliant and boring. I found it very hard to take the man seriously because it was more him than he was himself. A very interesting performance. Of equal interest is David Caker as Phillip Steele, Crisp's long time friend and confidant. Unfortunately much of the film is far from memory to me and I am not certain that it gets the details right. It does in fact manage to capture some of the real looks and feels of New York and its environs, but mostly its just an inert film of Crisp talking to people being witty, trying to come to terms with the world as it is (he is clearly regretting some of his decisions concerning AIDS) and coping with the infirmities that old age thrust upon him. Crisp's life is very interesting, but his life as portrayed here is not. I am a huge Crisp fan and have always admired the man and his unique point of view. I just wish he had lived to see this film about his life

This Dick Powell-directed film is based on the kind of story I loved as a teenager, but now find rather depressing. It's about the kind of age-based romantic attachments, where it is on the part of the elder person motivated by lust, or an inability to face the reality of aging, or both. And the younger person is just looking for the kind parent figure she (or he) lacked as a child. These stories often seem more pathetic than romantic to me, but there is also something rather intriguing about them. Dick Powell looked a bit embarrassed--as perhaps he should have--as the elder lover, a screenwriter. He was, at fifty, playing the part of a thirty-eight-year-old man romancing a teen-ager. But young Debbie Reynolds was a revelation--smart and saucy, full of vinegar--as a seventeen-year-old girl who sees herself as a kind of "project" for the morally confused and insecure screenwriter, as a subject for him to study. Her spirited performance alone earns from me a higher rating than the film might otherwise deserve. Anne Baxter was cast as Powell's beautiful, but shallow fiancée, and played her small part deftly. Some of the dialogue is rather amusing, too, so it's not a total washout. 5/6

I have no idea how accurate this portrayal of Flynn appears to be, but even as a work of fiction it is one of the worst films I have ever seen. The plot is all over the place and leaves you wondering how you got from one scene to the next. There are just too many characters and events needed to keep track of Flynn and his current situation, and it is difficult to understand Flynn's and other characters' motivations for some of their actions. Add to that a series of silly and implausible events and you have something that comes across as one of your dreams that seems to make sense while you are asleep, but when you wake up and you try to remember it, it is just strange, confusing, and completely unrealistic. There are many long and boring musical sections in the film that to me look like poor direction or a bad director, and not creative or artistic choice. All the characters are one-dimensional, especially Flynn, who comes across as a self serving bully, thug, thief, robber, murderer, addict, gambler, gigolo, and drug addict who will do anything and step on anyone to advance his own interests, yet somehow, despite all that, great opportunities always seem to miraculously fall into his lap. This film is not entertaining or satisfying in any way and by all accounts not even well made, so don't watch it. To add salt to the wound, the DVD was one of the worst transfers I have ever seen, it wasn't even in wide-screen or Dolby 5.1, it had a lot of static, his grain, and artifacts from what looked like a film reel that had been gathering dust somewhere..

Creakiness and atmosphere this film has, but so unfortunately does the print I just viewed. Raymond Massey provides a laid back Sherlock Holmes, almost comically so in early scenes in his bathrobe, which he trades in for a laborer's garb to investigate the creepy mansion of Dr. Rylott (Lyn Harding). What wasn't clear to me was why Rylott would have wanted his stepdaughters dead. If as in the case of Helen (Angela Baddeley), he didn't want her to run off to get married, he would have accomplished the same thing by having her dispatched. Other curiosities abound as well. After setting an early wedding date with Helen, the fiancée is no longer heard from for the rest of the picture. The presence of a band of gypsies at the time of Violet Stoner's death provides merely a diversion, and what could have been an interesting murder tool, a poisonous snake, is diluted by the fact that it was not a cobra, the musical renderings of the Indian man servant notwithstanding. Athole Stewart competently portrays Holmes' aide Dr. Watson, though he takes some getting used to if Nigel Bruce is more your cup of tea. As Rylott, Lyn Harding is sufficiently menacing, a trait that would be put to good use as Holmes' nemesis Professor Moriarty in two later films - 1935's "The Triumph of Sherlock Holmes" and 1937's "Murder at the Baskervilles". With repeated choppiness and an unsteady camera, it's surprising that the story line isn't more disrupted than it is. It's integrity is generally maintained, even if one stretches a bit to fill in the gaps. I guess that would be my main complaint with the film, as mentally bridging some of the jump cuts in the picture proved to be a real pain in the asp.

Though a fan of horror and gore, I found Jack Brooks VI to be... very disappointing. The effects and special effects were good, and some of the humor was well-timed, but... something was missing. Essentially, the first half of the film is exploring the nuances of Jack Brooks' personality, despite the fact that everything we need to know about his aggression is conveyed within one of the first title cards. As for the narration and the use of flashbacks: needless to say, the pacing during the second half is tedious. Most of it is focused on Freddy Krueger eating, then sleeping, and eating some more, then flailing his arms and saying his name once or twice. All the while, this schlock is intermixed with brief scenes of Jack discussing his relationship problems with his girlfriend. Definitely some entertaining moments in the film -- for example, some of the monsters that appear without explanation, and the caricatures of the monsters that are both hilarious and over-the-top. All in all, as a film that attempts to capture the spirit of classic horror movies, Jack Brooks: Monster Slayer has plenty of potential but ultimately fallsanders and drags on without delivering an adequate conclusion. Hopefully, though, these issues will be addressed before Jack Brooks VII: Jack vs. Hell or Jack vs. God goes into production
